hints: Look closely at the word formation and joining. What do we call the reaction that links two small sugar monomers together to make a bigger molecule?

Remember condensation versus hydrolysis for carbohydrates. Think about what is removed when two OH groups interact to make a C-O-C glycosidic link, and why a 1,6 link is also possible for alpha-glucose.
walkthrough:
**Spot the type of reaction**

Joining two alpha-glucose molecules together is building up, not breaking down. That tells us it is a condensation (synthesis) reaction, not hydrolysis.

Think: monomers join to form maltose or longer polysaccharides like starch.

**Recall what condensation always does**

In condensation, an OH from one glucose and an H from an OH on the other glucose are removed. They combine to release one small molecule.

Key rule:
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O$$

**Check what is always true**

Water is always released, but the position of the bond is not always 1,4. Two alpha-glucose molecules can also form a 1,6 bond at a branch point, as in amylopectin and glycogen. So only C is always correct.

options.A: Not always true. Alpha-glucose can form 1,4 links in a straight chain, but also 1,6 links at branch points in amylopectin and glycogen.
options.B: Incorrect. A glycosidic bond is a strong covalent C-O-C bond, not a weak hydrogen bond between molecules.
options.C: Correct and always true. Formation by condensation always removes H and OH to release one molecule of water for each new glycosidic bond.
options.D: Opposite of what happens. Hydroxyl groups are used up (lost as part of water), not formed, when the bond is made.
